chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad al-Bazzaz, from Zakariyya al-Mu'min, from Ishaq al-Sayrafi, who said:

I said to Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him): 'A man entered into ihram and trimmed his nails; one of his fingers was injured, so he left its nail untrimmed. After he had entered ihram, a man gave him a fatwa to trim it, so he trimmed it and it bled.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon the one who gave the fatwa is the blood money of a sheep.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And whoever shaves his head due to an affliction that befalls him, upon him is the blood money of a sheep, or feeding six poor people, for each poor person two mudds of food, or fasting three days.'

key_terms.إحرام: State of consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a pilgrim who shaves their head due to an affliction while in ihram?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the specific expiation for unintentional violations of ihram restrictions, such as trimming nails or shaving the head due to necessity or affliction. It highlights the scholarly distinction between the liability of the mufti who issued the permissive ruling and the pilgrim who acted upon it, assigning the penalty to the mufti in cases of error. The hadith establishes a flexible kaffarah structure—sacrificing a sheep, feeding six poor people, or fasting three days—reflecting the practical jurisprudence of the Ahl al-Bayt regarding minor infractions during Hajj.
